name: Fitness Classes: Yoga
description:
Class Description: Embodied Flow This one-hour yoga experience blends Vinyasa flow and Pilates-inspired movement to cultivate strength, balance, and release. Each class begins with a moment of intention-setting, inviting you to ground your energy and arrive fully in the body. By integrating breath, presence, and intentional movement, students are guided to move with awareness and acceptance. Sessions emphasize core strength, stability, and increased range of motion. Students of all levels are welcome.

Truth is found in the breath.

Fitness Classes are open to all students, staff and faculty! There is no need to sign up for the class, just arrive 5 minutes before the start of class and bring some water! name: Cultural Exchanges between Greece and India
description:
Cultural Exchanges between Greece and India 
The lecture will be an exploration of how the ancient Greeks reacted to, represented, and interacted with India. After a brief introduction to the earliest accounts (Herodotus, Ctesias), we will focus on the expedition of Alexander the Great in India and its major literary sources (especially Arrian). We will also briefly touch on how those accounts influenced later representations of India in Roman times and beyond.

description:
Co-sponsored by Health Professions Advising and the Career Development Office

Join admissions representatives from the Johns Hopkins University School of Nursing and the University of Pennsylvania School of Nursing for an in-person information session exploring pathways into the nursing profession through accelerated entry programs.

Representatives will provide an overview of their nationally recognized nursing programs, including accelerated Master of Nursing and other graduate entry pathways for students who have completed a bachelor's degree in another discipline. The session will also discuss admissions requirements, prerequisite coursework, clinical training, financial aid, career opportunities, and what distinguishes each institution's approach to nursing education.

Students considering careers in nursing, advanced practice nursing, public health, or healthcare leadership are encouraged to attend. This is an excellent opportunity to learn about the profession, ask questions directly of admissions officers, and gain insights into preparing a competitive application.

Smith, MD, Associate Medical Director for Primary Care at Ochsner Health, in conversation with Soka University of America Student Fellow Kiarra Hoes.

Co-hosted by Soka University of America and the WHO Collaborating Centre for Healthy Cities and Urban Policy Research at the Institute of Science Tokyo, the Humanism & Health Speaker Series examines how health professionals and leaders translate humanistic values into practice across clinical care, health systems, public and global health, and planetary health. name: Annotations of Hope: Dr. Nahum Chandler on Du Bois's "Of the Coming of John"
description:
A lecture by Dr. Nahum Chandler

W. E. B. Du Bois’s short story “Of the Coming of John “is about a young man’s journey, from a happy go lucky small-town boy with never a care in the world, through an initial failure in his first year of college, to his return to school and discovery of himself anew in the world of thought. It is the discovery of what Du Bois elsewhere describes as a kind of “double-consciousness.” This short story is the masterpiece of Du Bois’s book The Souls of Black Folk: Essays and Sketches of 1903, a classic text in American thought — a book and short story about hope for the future of America at the turn to the 20th century.
 
The story is about 20 pages long. An audio version is available. The text can be found online in a reliable scholarly edition, including through Ikeda Library. Please read or listen before the lecture. Music as reference and hearing will be integral to the lecture.

name: Asian Americas: Discussing Papers from Graduate Students at CalState Los Angeles
description:
Two graduate students from CalState Los Angeles, both focusing on Asian migrant communities, will share their research in a conference-style environment with SUA students, especially Intro to the Pacific Basin (which will have a field trip a few days later on a related themes). SUA undergraduates will serve as discussants, followed by a dinner at the cafeteria to discuss grad studies in Los Angeles. Paper/author info below.

The event is co-sponsored by the Pacific Basin Area and the Pacific Basin Research Center.

Ari Muramoto, “Exclusion by Dispatch: Chinese Belonging and the Limits of Antichinismo in Guadalajara, 1920–1931”
Anti-Chinese violence erupted along Mexico’s northern borders in 1911, where campaigns pushed to expel their communities. Historians have argued that Mexico’s anti-Chinese movement mirrored California’s. Using the El Informador newspaper coverage from 1920-1931, this paper shifts the focus of the Anti-Chinese movement to Guadalajara, Jalisco, where the movement did not take hold. The Unión Fraternal China de Guadalajara was one of many Chinese Nationalist Party branches, that modeled their governing structure to the party in Nanjing. El Informador featured the Unión Fraternal anniversary celebrations of the Republic of China, elected party members, and delegate meetings. While maintaining their connection to their homeland, Chinese community members were assimilating into local society, marrying Mexican women, participating in Catholic rites, becoming prominent merchants and bankers, and appearing in newspaper society pages. At the same time, the El Informador printed petitions for expulsion and reported the Sonora campaign. While loyal to China yet integrated into Guadalajara's social life, this community contradicted the antichinismo claim that Chinese people could never become Mexican. Guadalajara demonstrates that Mexico’s antichinismo depended on who held local power, and that the California model, however relevant for borderlands, cannot explain the anti-Chinese movement in Mexico as a whole.

Henry Truong, “Desert Donuts: An Oral History of Vietnamese Refugee Resettlement in the California Desert”
The late stages of the Vietnam War resulted in sizable Vietnamese refugee communities. In the United States, ethnic enclaves emerged in Orange County, California; San Jose, California; Houston, Texas; and Seattle, Washington. However, documenting the experiences of Vietnamese refugees who settled outside of these major enclaves contributes to the broader history of Vietnamese resettlement in the United States. The purpose of this oral history project is to document the experiences of a Vietnamese refugee family that settled in a rural desert community in the United States after leaving Vietnam. Through recorded interviews with first-generation refugees and 1.5-generation immigrants, this project documents life in pre-war and wartime Vietnam, the displacement process, the journey to the United States, cultural adaptation in a new country, and the family’s experiences in a desert community that is part rural community, part military town. This project preserves personal narratives about the conditions that led to their displacement and how the family found a new life as fixtures of the local business community.
